name: Gum arabic and Indian ink eyebrow darkener

card.summary: A homemade brow-darkening mixture of acacia gum and ink painted onto sparse or pale brows to make them look fuller and darker.
card.aka: DIY brow tint, homemade brow ink
card.note: Ink not made for skin may irritate; permanent cosmetic pigment can require laser removal.

quick.overview:
This is a do-it-yourself brow product in which dark ink is combined with gum arabic, a water-soluble tree gum, to make a paint that is brushed onto the eyebrow. The aim is a darker, more defined brow that photographs and reads as fuller from a distance.

Gum arabic is a traditional binder for watercolour and ink and an ingredient in some cosmetics, which is the reasoning behind the mixture: the gum helps the colour stay on the hair and skin. No studies have tested homemade ink-and-gum brow paints.
quick.how: People paint the mixture onto the brow with a fine brush, in the manner of a brow pomade or tint, building colour in sparse areas. Commercial alternatives include pencils, powders, gels, salon tints and cosmetic tattooing.
quick.risks: Inks made for drawing are not formulated or tested for skin near the eyes, so irritation or allergic reaction is possible. Where pigment is deposited into skin rather than painted on, as in cosmetic eyebrow tattoos, removal has required laser treatment in published case series.

lead: Gum arabic and Indian ink eyebrow darkener is a homemade brow colourant: dark ink mixed with gum arabic, the dried sap of Acacia trees, and applied to the brows to deepen and fill them.[1] Gum arabic is a water-soluble mixture of polysaccharides and glycoproteins that serves as the traditional binder for watercolour paint, controls viscosity in inks, and is used as an adhesive and as a binder in some cosmetics.[1]

Its role in appearance is straightforward: eyebrows that are pale, sparse or patchy look fuller and more defined when darkened, and pencils, powders, gels, dye tinting and cosmetic tattooing are all used to that end.[2] The gum-and-ink recipe is a DIY version in the same family.

No clinical studies of this particular mixture have been published. Related literature covers cosmetic eyebrow tattoos, whose removal in a 2020 pilot study of four patients used a picosecond laser.[3]

chain: Ink and gum painted on the brow
Sparse or pale hair appears darker and fuller
More defined brow frame around the eyes
angle.text: Like any brow colour, the mixture adds visible pigment to the hair and skin, so thin or light brows look denser and darker while the colour lasts.

paras: Gum arabic is harvested mainly in Sudan and the Sahel and dissolves readily in water; it is used in watercolours, inks, stamps' adhesive, candies, soft drinks and pharmaceuticals.[1] Adding it to ink gives a paint-like consistency, which is the rationale given for using it as a brow paint.
Mainstream brow products include pencils, brushes and shaders, gels and powders matched to natural hair colour, permanent dye tinting and tattooing or microblading.[2]

Ink intended for drawing is not made for use on skin near the eyes. Cosmetic eyebrow tattoos, a permanent pigment option, can be removed with laser: a 2020 pilot study reported successful removal in four patients with skin types III-IV using a picosecond laser with a perfluorodecalin-infused patch.[3]
No studies found. Related research on removing cosmetic eyebrow tattoos is limited to small case series such as a four-patient pilot study.[3]

refs.title: Successful Treatment of Cosmetic Eyebrow Tattoos in Fitzpatrick III-IV With Picosecond Nd:YAG Laser With a Perfluorodecalin-Infused Patch: A Pilot Study
